Against the Presumption of Violent Resistance: Why Persecution Alone Cannot Justify Taking Up Arms

Introduction

Throughout history, ethnic and religious minorities have endured unconscionable persecution at the hands of governments sworn to protect all their citizens. From pogroms to ethnic cleansing, from discriminatory legislation to outright massacre, the catalogue of state-sponsored violence against vulnerable populations is both long and harrowing. In the face of such horrors, a seemingly instinctive moral calculus emerges: if a government attacks its own people on the basis of their identity, those people are justified in taking up arms. This reasoning feels intuitive, even obvious. It appeals to the deepest human instincts of self-preservation and justice.

Yet I contend that persecution by a government, however severe, is not by itself a sufficient justification for violent resistance. This is not a claim that persecuted minorities lack moral standing, nor that their suffering is trivial, nor that they bear any blame for the atrocities committed against them. Rather, it is the more precise claim that the bare fact of being attacked does not automatically render violent response the morally permissible course. Justification for organized violence requires a far more comprehensive moral accounting—one that weighs probable consequences, exhausts alternatives, considers proportionality, and honestly reckons with the likely outcomes for the very community such violence purports to defend. To conflate the right to be free from persecution with the right to wage armed struggle is to collapse a complex moral question into a dangerous oversimplification.

I. The Moral Weight of Consequences

The most fundamental problem with treating government persecution as a standalone justification for violent resistance is that such reasoning is entirely backward-looking. It asks only, "Have we been wronged?" without ever asking, "Will violence make things better?" Moral reasoning that ignores consequences is incomplete at best and reckless at worst.

History provides a sobering record on this point. For every successful armed resistance by a persecuted minority, there are dozens of cases where violent response led to escalated repression, collective punishment, and catastrophic loss of life within the very community the violence was meant to protect. When small, outgunned minority populations take up arms against the apparatus of a modern state, the asymmetry of power almost invariably produces devastating results. Governments facing armed internal resistance frequently use that resistance as a pretext to intensify persecution, to justify martial law, to rally majority populations against the minority in question, and to reframe systematic oppression as legitimate counterterrorism or national security.

The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943 is often invoked as the paradigmatic case of justified violent resistance—and the moral courage of its participants is beyond question. Yet it must be honestly acknowledged that the uprising did not save the Jewish population of Warsaw. The ghetto was destroyed. Nearly all of its remaining inhabitants were killed. The uprising served a profound symbolic and dignitary function, and one may argue that its participants chose the manner of their death rather than its fact. But if the question is whether violence improved outcomes for the persecuted community, the answer is far less clear. Symbolism and dignity matter enormously, but they do not constitute a sufficient justification framework for decisions that determine whether thousands of people live or die.

A consequentialist assessment demands that we ask uncomfortable questions. Will violent resistance provoke a crackdown that kills more community members than it saves? Will it alienate potential allies in the majority population? Will it provide propaganda victories to the persecuting regime? Will it destabilize the region in ways that produce further suffering? Will it destroy the social infrastructure—the schools, religious institutions, community networks—that sustain the minority's identity and survival? If the honest answers to these questions suggest that violence will produce worse outcomes for the persecuted group, then persecution alone has not justified the resort to arms. Something more is needed: a reasonable prospect that violence will actually achieve protective or liberatory aims.

II. The Obligation to Exhaust Alternatives

Just war theory, in both its secular and religious formulations, has long insisted that war must be a last resort. This principle applies with equal or greater force to the question of violent resistance by persecuted minorities. Before organized violence can be morally countenanced, there must be a genuine reckoning with whether nonviolent alternatives have been attempted, exhausted, or rendered genuinely impossible.

The twentieth and twenty-first centuries have furnished extraordinary evidence for the efficacy of nonviolent resistance, even under conditions of severe state repression. The Indian independence movement under Gandhi's leadership, the American Civil Rights Movement under Martin Luther King Jr., the Solidarity movement in Poland, the People Power Revolution in the Philippines, the anti-apartheid movement in South Africa (which, while it included an armed wing, achieved its decisive victories through economic pressure, international solidarity, and mass nonviolent mobilization)—these movements demonstrate that nonviolent strategies can succeed even against governments willing to employ brutal force.

Erica Chenoweth and Maria Stephan's landmark study, Why Civil Resistance Works, analyzed 323 violent and nonviolent resistance campaigns between 1900 and 2006 and found that nonviolent campaigns succeeded 53 percent of the time, compared to 26 percent for violent campaigns. Moreover, nonviolent campaigns were far more likely to lead to durable democratic governance afterward. The reasons are instructive: nonviolent movements lower the barriers to participation, enabling larger and more diverse coalitions; they create loyalty shifts among security forces and regime supporters; they generate greater international sympathy and support; and they avoid the cycle of reprisal and counter-reprisal that tends to entrench authoritarian power.

None of this means that nonviolent resistance is easy, painless, or guaranteed to succeed. It demands extraordinary courage, discipline, and willingness to suffer. It can take years or decades. But the argument that persecution by a government alone justifies violent resistance implicitly dismisses these alternatives without examination. It assumes that because the injustice is severe, the most extreme response is automatically warranted. This is a non sequitur. The severity of the wrong tells us something about the urgency of response but nothing about which form of response is most justified.

A persecuted minority that has not attempted organized civil disobedience, international appeals, documentation of atrocities for the global community, economic leverage, coalition-building with sympathetic elements in the majority population, legal challenges, or strategic noncooperation cannot honestly claim that violence is the only remaining option. And if violence is not the only remaining option, then persecution alone has not justified it.

III. The Problem of Authority and Representation

When we speak of a minority "resorting to violent resistance," we often speak as though the minority is a unified actor with a single will. In reality, the decision to pursue armed struggle is almost always made by a subset of the community—often young men, often organized into militant factions that may or may not represent the broader community's wishes or interests.

This raises a profound moral problem. On whose authority is violence undertaken? The bare fact of government persecution does not automatically confer upon any particular faction the right to make life-and-death decisions on behalf of an entire community. When a militant group launches attacks in the name of an ethnic or religious minority, it is the entire minority that bears the consequences—the reprisals, the collective punishment, the loss of whatever fragile protections or alliances may have existed. The elderly, the children, the women, the disabled, the moderate, the pacifist—all are implicated in a decision they may not have endorsed and cannot escape.

History is replete with cases where militant factions claiming to act on behalf of a persecuted group made strategic and moral choices that proved catastrophic for the broader community. The resort to violence can empower the most extreme elements within a minority, marginalizing moderates and pragmatists whose strategies might have been more effective. It can create internal power struggles that fracture community solidarity. It can produce warlordism, criminality, and authoritarian structures within the resistance itself that become new sources of oppression.

The argument that government persecution alone justifies violent resistance elides these questions of internal legitimacy entirely. It treats the move from "we are being attacked" to "therefore we may fight" as though it requires no additional moral infrastructure—no process of collective deliberation, no mechanism of accountability, no standard of representativeness. But organized violence undertaken without legitimate authority is not resistance; it is freelance warfare conducted at the expense of the community it claims to serve.

IV. Proportionality and the Targeting Problem

Even if we accept that some form of forceful response to persecution may sometimes be warranted, the claim that persecution alone justifies violence glosses over the inescapable question of what kind of violence, directed at whom. Just war theory requires proportionality and discrimination—the distinction between legitimate and illegitimate targets. These requirements do not evaporate simply because the cause is sympathetic.

When persecuted minorities resort to organized violence, the practical realities of asymmetric conflict frequently erode these moral boundaries. Lacking the capacity to engage government military forces directly, insurgent groups often turn to tactics that deliberately or foreseeably harm civilians: bombings in public spaces, assassinations that provoke collective reprisals, attacks on infrastructure that affects entire populations. The logic of escalation, the pressure of survival, and the intoxicating moral certainty that comes from genuine victimhood can combine to produce atrocities committed by the oppressed that mirror—or in specific instances exceed—those committed by the oppressor.

This is not a hypothetical concern. It is an observable pattern. Groups that begin with legitimate grievances, whose communities have suffered genuine persecution, have repeatedly crossed moral lines that no amount of prior suffering can sanction. The suffering of one's community does not grant permission to target another community's civilians. The persecution of one's people does not authorize the murder of children on a school bus, the bombing of a marketplace, or the massacre of villagers who happen to share the ethnicity of the ruling regime.

The argument that persecution alone justifies violence provides no internal limiting principle. If the fact of being attacked is sufficient, then any response becomes permissible, because any response can be characterized as resistance to attack. The absence of additional criteria—proportionality, discrimination, reasonable prospect of success, legitimate authority—transforms justified grievance into a blank check for unlimited violence. This is morally untenable.

V. The Corruption of the Community's Moral Identity

There is a subtler but no less important cost to violent resistance that the persecution-as-justification argument fails to reckon with: the effect of organized violence on the moral identity and social fabric of the community that wages it.

Communities that organize around armed struggle undergo profound internal transformations. Military logic displaces civic logic. Hierarchies of violence replace hierarchies of wisdom, learning, or spiritual authority. Children are socialized into cultures of martyrdom and vengeance. Trauma is not only suffered but actively perpetuated. The skills, habits, and institutional structures developed during armed conflict persist long after the conflict ends, producing societies scarred by militarism, intolerance of dissent, and cycles of retributive violence.

Martin Luther King Jr. understood this with piercing clarity when he argued that "the ultimate weakness of violence is that it is a descending spiral, begetting the very thing it seeks to destroy." King was not speaking from a position of safety or abstraction. He was a Black man in the American South, subject to daily threats, physical attacks, and the ever-present possibility of assassination—which ultimately claimed his life. He watched his community suffer under the boot of state-sanctioned racial terror. Yet he insisted that violent resistance would corrode the moral character of the movement and the community, producing a pyrrhic liberation that preserved the structures of hatred even as it dismantled the structures of law.

This is not merely a strategic calculation; it is a moral one. A community that defines itself through armed struggle risks losing the very identity it sought to protect. The traditions, values, cultural practices, and modes of being that constitute a minority's distinctive existence can be consumed by the all-encompassing demands of warfare. Victory, if it comes, may arrive too late—after the community has been transformed into something unrecognizable, having adopted the methods and mentality of its oppressor.

VI. The International and Intergenerational Dimensions

The claim that persecution justifies violence also fails to account for the broader relational context in which minorities exist. Ethnic and religious minorities do not live in isolation. They exist alongside other communities, within regional and international systems, across generational time. Violent resistance sends shockwaves through all of these dimensions in ways that the persecution-as-justification argument does not address.

Regionally, armed conflict by a minority group frequently destabilizes neighboring areas, produces refugee crises, draws in external actors with their own agendas, and ignites sympathetic conflicts elsewhere. The violence undertaken by one persecuted group can be instrumentalized by great powers, arms dealers, and opportunistic political actors in ways that compound suffering far beyond the original community.

Internationally, the resort to violence can undermine the diplomatic, legal, and moral frameworks that represent persecuted minorities' best long-term hope for protection. The development of international human rights law, the International Criminal Court, the Responsibility to Protect doctrine, and global civil society networks all depend on the maintenance of norms that distinguish between legitimate and illegitimate uses of force. When persecuted minorities adopt methods indistinguishable from terrorism, they weaken the very normative architecture that could protect them and others like them.

Intergenerationally, the decision to pursue violent resistance creates path dependencies that constrain the choices of future generations. Children raised in conflict zones, educated in the ideology of armed struggle, and traumatized by violence and loss carry those experiences forward in ways that perpetuate cycles of conflict long after the original persecution has ended or transformed. The moral calculus of violent resistance cannot be limited to the present generation's suffering; it must account for the world bequeathed to those who come after.

VII. Addressing the Strongest Counterargument

The strongest counterargument to my position is the case of genocide—the systematic attempt to exterminate an entire people. Surely, when a government is actively engaged in genocide, the targeted group is justified in using any means necessary to survive, and the academic weighing of alternatives becomes obscene in the face of gas chambers and mass graves.

I take this objection with the utmost seriousness, and I want to be precise about what I am and am not claiming. I am not arguing that violent self-defense is never justified. I am not arguing that a person or community facing imminent extermination must submit passively to death. I am arguing that the fact of government persecution, standing alone and without further moral analysis, is not a sufficient justification for organized violent resistance.

Even in the most extreme cases, the additional analysis may be conducted swiftly and may yield a clear answer. When genocide is underway, when no international intervention is forthcoming, when nonviolent alternatives have been foreclosed by the totality of the assault, when violence offers a genuine prospect of saving lives, when it can be conducted with some degree of proportionality and discrimination—then the full moral case for violent resistance may well be satisfied. But it is satisfied by the conjunction of these factors, not by persecution alone. The additional criteria are not bureaucratic obstacles; they are the moral reasoning that distinguishes justified resistance from aimless or counterproductive violence.

Moreover, the genocide case is the extreme end of a vast spectrum. Most situations involving government persecution of minorities, however severe, fall short of active extermination. They involve discrimination, dispossession, imprisonment, sporadic violence, cultural suppression, and political marginalization. These are grave injustices that demand urgent response. But the appropriate response varies enormously depending on circumstances, and the automatic equation of persecution with justification for violence collapses critically important distinctions.

Conclusion

To argue that government persecution of an ethnic or religious minority is not, by itself, a sufficient justification for violent resistance is not to excuse persecution or to counsel passivity. It is to insist that moral reasoning must be complete rather than truncated. The decision to resort to organized violence—to kill and to accept the killing that will inevitably follow—is among the gravest decisions any community can make. It demands a comprehensive moral framework that accounts for consequences, alternatives, authority, proportionality, effects on community identity, and obligations to future generations.

Persecuted minorities deserve justice, protection, solidarity, and the full recognition of their humanity and rights. They deserve the vigorous intervention of the international community, the enforcement of human rights law, and the moral and material support of people of conscience everywhere. What they do not deserve is a facile moral formula that equates their suffering with a license for violence—a formula that may, in practice, lead them into greater suffering while absolving the rest of us of our responsibility to offer them better options.

The measure of our moral seriousness is not whether we reflexively endorse the most dramatic response to injustice, but whether we have the patience and rigor to pursue the response most likely to end it. Violence may sometimes be part of that response. But the argument for it must be made with a full accounting of its costs, its alternatives, and its consequences—not simply by pointing to the undeniable reality that a terrible wrong has been committed. Terrible wrongs demand effective responses, and effectiveness is a standard that the mere fact of persecution, however harrowing, cannot by itself establish.

The Unyielding Power of Peace: A Call to Non-Violent Resistance

Brothers and sisters, friends, fellow human beings—

I stand before you today with a heart that is heavy, but a spirit that is unbroken.

We have witnessed what no person of conscience should ever have to witness. We have seen our neighbors dragged from their homes. We have seen houses of worship desecrated. We have seen laws twisted into weapons and institutions corrupted into instruments of cruelty. We have seen a government—a body sworn to protect all of its people—turn its machinery of power against those whose only crime is their identity, their faith, or the blood running through their veins.

And in the face of such monstrous injustice, every fiber of our being cries out: Fight back.

I understand that cry. I feel that cry. It lives in my chest as it lives in yours.

But I am here today to ask you—no, to implore you—to fight back in the way that history has proven most powerful, most enduring, and most transformative. I am here to call you to the discipline of non-violent resistance—not because our suffering doesn't matter, but precisely because it does.

Let me be absolutely clear about what I am NOT saying.

I am not saying that the persecution is acceptable. It is an abomination.

I am not saying that our pain is exaggerated. It is immeasurable.

I am not saying we should be passive. Passivity is surrender, and I will never ask you to surrender.

I am not saying we should be silent. Our voices will shake the foundations of injustice until those foundations crack and crumble into dust.

What I AM saying is this: the fact that a government has committed violence against us does not, by itself, make violence the right answer. An injustice inflicted upon us does not automatically sanctify every response we might choose. Our cause is righteous—but righteousness of cause does not guarantee righteousness of method.

We must be more disciplined than that. We must be more strategic than that. And ultimately, we must be more courageous than that.

Consider the arithmetic of violence.

When an armed government attacks an unarmed minority, they hold every advantage of force. They have the soldiers. They have the weapons. They have the prisons and the courts and the bureaucracies of control. If we answer their violence with violence, we are fighting on their terrain, by their rules, with their advantages.

And worse—far worse—we hand them the very narrative they need. Every stone we throw becomes their justification. Every act of retaliation becomes their evening news. "You see?" they will tell the world. "You see what kind of people they are? We were right to fear them. We were right to contain them." The moment we raise our fists, we transform ourselves in the eyes of the undecided from victims of oppression into participants in a conflict. And in a conflict between a government and a minority, the world will often look away.

We cannot afford to let them look away.

But non-violence is not weakness. Let no one ever tell you it is weakness.

It takes no courage to strike back in anger. Anger is easy. Rage is reflexive. Any human being cornered and beaten will lash out—it is instinct, it is animal, it is automatic.

But to stand in the face of batons, to sit when they demand you run, to link arms when they bring dogs, to sing when they bring guns, to return to the streets the morning after they have beaten you the night before—that requires a courage so profound it terrifies the oppressor far more than any weapon ever could.

Because they know how to fight violence. They have trained for it. They have budgeted for it. They have built entire institutions around it.

They do not know how to fight a people who refuse to be provoked.

When Gandhi led the Salt March, the British Empire—the most powerful force on Earth—did not fall to bullets. It fell to the image of unarmed Indians walking calmly into the clubs of soldiers, rising, and walking forward again. The conscience of the world could not look at that and remain unmoved.

When John Lewis walked across the Edmund Pettus Bridge, when the dogs and fire hoses of Birmingham were turned on children who held no weapons, when Rosa Parks simply stayed in her seat—the moral bankruptcy of segregation was exposed not by an opposing army, but by the unassailable dignity of those who refused to become what their oppressors accused them of being.

When the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo walked in silent circles, week after week, year after year, wearing white headscarves and carrying photographs of their disappeared children, no army could defeat them—because there was nothing to defeat. There was only truth, walking in circles, refusing to be erased.

I hear the objection. I hear it because I have asked it myself in the darkest hours of the night.

"But they are killing us. They are killing us now. How can you ask us to remain peaceful while our people die?"

I do not ask it lightly. I ask it with trembling hands and tears I have not finished shedding.

But I ask you: will our violence stop the killing? Or will it multiply it? History answers this question with brutal clarity. When a persecuted minority takes up arms against its government, the government rarely backs down. Instead, it escalates. It points to the violence as proof of the threat. It consolidates public support. Moderate voices within the government who might have been allies are silenced by the drums of war. International sympathy evaporates as the narrative shifts from persecution to civil conflict.

The mathematics of suffering do not improve when we add our own violence to the equation. They only compound.

And let us speak honestly about what violence does to us—to our own souls, to our own communities. Violence does not only destroy the enemy. It transforms the one who wields it. When we organize around violence, we must build hierarchies of command. We must enforce discipline through fear. We must silence dissent within our own ranks. We begin to mirror the very structures that oppress us. We become, in the name of liberation, a new kind of prison.

The revolution that liberates the body while imprisoning the spirit is no revolution at all.

So what do I propose? What does non-violent resistance look like when the boot is on your neck?

It looks like documentation. Every injustice recorded. Every name remembered. Every photograph, every testimony, every piece of evidence preserved and shared with the world. In the age of information, truth is a weapon more powerful than any rifle.

It looks like solidarity. When they come for one community, all communities respond. We find allies among the majority population—and they exist, they always exist—people of conscience who know that what is done to the least of us is done to all of us. We make the oppressor's task impossible by dissolving the lines they have drawn between us.

It looks like non-cooperation. General strikes. Economic boycotts. Tax resistance. The withdrawal of consent and labor from systems that depend upon our participation to function. Let the gears of the machine grind to a halt when we remove ourselves from them.

It looks like international pressure. Appeals to courts, to organizations, to governments, to the global public. Shame is a powerful force when those who wield it stand on unimpeachable moral ground.

It looks like civil disobedience. The deliberate, open, peaceful breaking of unjust laws—and the willingness to accept the consequences. When the prisons are full of people whose only crime was peacefully asserting their humanity, the world cannot help but ask: what kind of government is this?

It looks like showing up. Day after day after day. When they disperse you on Monday, you return on Tuesday. When they arrest you in the morning, your neighbors march in the afternoon. You demonstrate to the oppressor a truth they cannot comprehend: you cannot imprison an idea, you cannot beat conviction out of a people, and you cannot kill a movement that has already decided it is willing to die but never willing to kill.

I will not pretend the path I describe is easy. It is the hardest path there is.

Non-violence demands more of us than violence ever could. It demands patience when every nerve screams for action. It demands discipline when chaos feels justified. It demands faith—not necessarily in God, though many of us draw strength from that well—but faith in the fundamental decency that lives somewhere in every human heart, even hearts that have been corrupted by power and prejudice.

It demands that we see our oppressors as human beings—not because they have earned that recognition, but because our humanity depends on our ability to grant it. The moment we dehumanize those who dehumanize us, we have lost the very thing we are fighting to protect.

Some will call us naive. Let them.

History is on our side. The British Empire fell not to the armies of colonized peoples, but to their organized, persistent, unyielding non-cooperation. Apartheid did not end because the oppressed outgunned the oppressor; it ended because the moral weight of resistance, of boycotts, of international solidarity, became too heavy for the regime to bear. The Berlin Wall did not fall to artillery; it fell to candles, to prayers, to people simply walking through.

The victories of violence are temporary. The victories of non-violence reshape the moral landscape of civilization itself.

My brothers and sisters—

We did not choose this fight. It was brought to our doorsteps, to our dinner tables, to our places of worship. We did not choose to be targets of our own government's cruelty.

But we can choose how we respond. And in that choice lies our greatest power.

They expect us to fight, so they can justify destroying us.

They expect us to flee, so they can erase us.

They expect us to submit, so they can forget us.

We will do none of these things.

We will resist. We will resist with every breath, every step, every voice raised in unison. We will resist with the most powerful force human civilization has ever known: the organized, unwavering, non-violent demand for justice.

We will fill their streets with our presence. We will fill their courts with our cases. We will fill their prisons with our bodies if we must. We will fill the conscience of the world with our story.

And we will win. Not today, perhaps. Not tomorrow. But we will win—because no government in the history of the world has ever permanently defeated a people who decided, together, that their dignity was non-negotiable and their methods would remain consistent with the world they were trying to build.

We are building a world where no government turns on its own people. We cannot build that world with the tools of destruction. We can only build it with the tools of creation—love, solidarity, courage, sacrifice, and the unshakeable conviction that every human being deserves to live in peace.

Stand with me. March with me. Resist with me.

But let us resist as the people we wish to become—not as reflections of those who oppress us.

The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice. Let us be the hands that bend it.

Together. Peacefully. Unbreakably.

Thank you.

Even when an ethnic or religious minority is attacked by its own government, violent resistance is not automatically justified. An attack by the state is a grave injustice and a violation of the government's most basic duty, but that fact alone is not sufficient moral or practical justification for responding with violence.

The first reason is strategic: violent resistance by a minority against a state almost always fails on its own terms and makes the minority's position worse.

A government, by definition, holds a near-monopoly on organized force, intelligence, logistics, and territorial control. When a minority takes up arms, it invites the state to do what it does best — wage war. What may begin as discriminatory policing, seizure of property, or targeted harassment can then be rebranded by the state as a necessary counter-insurgency operation. This shift is catastrophic for the minority. It allows the government to justify to the majority population and to the world a level of force that would have previously been seen as illegitimate. Curfews, mass detention, surveillance, and military deployment become framed not as oppression, but as security.

History is consistent on this point. Armed uprisings by outnumbered minorities do not preserve the community; they accelerate its destruction, create refugee crises, and give the state a pretext for collective punishment. The people who suffer most in the resulting war are not the government officials who ordered the attack, but the non-combatant members of the minority itself.

The second reason is moral and relates to legitimacy.

A minority attacked by its government possesses something immensely powerful: clear moral legitimacy. It is the victim of a wrong. That legitimacy is the foundation for everything that can actually produce lasting safety — legal challenges, internal dissent within the majority, external diplomatic pressure, economic sanctions, humanitarian aid, asylum, and international legal proceedings.

Violent resistance voluntarily surrenders that legitimacy. Once a minority movement uses violence, the conflict ceases in the public eye to be a story of an abused population seeking protection, and becomes a story of two armed factions fighting. The central moral question changes from "How do we stop the state from abusing its people?" to "Who shot first in this latest incident?" It forces third parties who might have been allies to remain neutral, and it alienates potential allies within the majority population who oppose their government's actions but will not support an armed insurrection.

The principle of just cause in any ethical framework for the use of force requires more than a wrong having occurred. It requires that violence be a last resort, that it have a reasonable prospect of success, and that it be proportional and discriminating — meaning it can avoid harming non-combatants. An ethnic or religious minority, surrounded and outgunned, cannot meet those criteria simply because it has been attacked. Anger and trauma are understandable human responses, but they are not a strategy and they do not by themselves satisfy the heavy burden required to justify taking up arms.

The third reason is that violence creates a cycle that outlives the original attack.

Government oppression wants to be seen as necessary. When a state attacks a minority, it often does so by claiming that minority is inherently dangerous, disloyal, or violent. A violent response retroactively validates that propaganda in the eyes of the majority, ensuring that prejudice hardens into permanent hatred. Children on both sides are raised in war. Even if the regime changes, the communal wounds inflicted during a period of mutual violence make reconciliation and coexistence far more difficult than recovering from one-sided oppression.

This is why the most effective movements for minority survival under oppression have been those that explicitly refused to meet state violence with communal violence. Nonviolent discipline is not passivity. It is an active strategy that keeps the focus on the government's actions, keeps the community united and alive, preserves leadership, and builds the broad coalitions necessary to force change. It denies the state the justification it most seeks.

Being attacked by one's government is a profound moral wrong. It deserves condemnation, accountability, and remedy. But the fact that a wrong has been committed does not automatically license any and all responses. Violent resistance, when judged by its consequences, its moral cost, and its likelihood of success, requires far more justification than the attack alone provides.
